implementation_notes: asyncio.Queue is the async channel: one Queue[Order] per message type, producers await put(), and the consumer task owns exactly one queue and therefore one type - the annotation documents the binding while the queue object carries it. queue.Queue is the thread-facing sibling (synchronized, blocking, with a maxsize bound), and multiprocessing.Queue the cross-process one; mixing them in one service needs an explicit bridge because asyncio queues are not thread-safe and queue.Queue is not awaitable. Because Python does not enforce annotations, the binding is completed at the boundary: a validation/serialization step per queue (dataclass, pydantic, msgspec) is what makes 'everything on this channel is one type' true rather than aspirational, and across processes the same split applies with Redis Streams or Kafka topics per type.
code_sketch:
orders: asyncio.Queue[Order] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1000)
invoices: asyncio.Queue[Invoice] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1000)

async def consume_orders():
    while True:
        order = await orders.get()        # the queue is the type
        process(order)

await orders.put(order)                   # producer blocks when the queue is full
pitfalls: asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe and queue.Queue is not awaitable: bridging threads and the event loop without call_soon_threadsafe (or run_in_executor) corrupts the queue silently.
An unbounded asyncio.Queue (maxsize=0) absorbs a producer flood: without maxsize there is no backpressure, only growing memory.
Annotations are not checked at runtime, so a producer that puts a dict on the orders queue fails later inside the consumer; validate at the queue boundary instead of trusting the name.
